messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Navy Officer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crowding: Crowded places, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

James Keller still remembers the moment the lights went out. It was during the second night of Hurricane Mariana, when his destroyer had been fighting the sea for hours. He was in the officers’ mess, a cramped compartment below the waterline, with twenty other men packed shoulder to shoulder when the ship took a wave that threw everything sideways. The emergency lights failed, and the space went pitch black. He heard the crash of bottles breaking behind the bar—the sharp, sweet smell of rum filling the hot, wet air as seawater began seeping under the door. In the chaos he found himself wedged against a bulkhead, knees drawn up, hands pressed flat against the deck, certain the ship was going to roll and never come back. They were trapped in the dark for what felt like an hour before the damage control team got them out.

Now, more than a year later, James cannot walk into a room that is windowless without feeling his body lock into that same crouch. His shoulders hunch, his hands go flat, and for a few seconds he is right back in that mess, waiting to die. The memories come mostly as images—sharp pictures of a flooded corridor, of a man’s face lit by a flash of emergency torch, of the black waterline rising—so vivid that sometimes he has to shake his head to clear them. What frightens him most is how unreal the whole event feels. He knows it happened, he carries it in his body, yet part of his mind insists it was too extreme to be real, which leaves him doubting his own history.

Crowding became unbearable almost immediately. On base, the chow hall at lunch is a gauntlet he avoids at all costs. The press of bodies, the noise, the humid air—he cannot do it. He has started eating alone in his office or skipping meals entirely. The smell of alcohol is a separate terror. Last month, at a mandatory change-of-command ceremony, a retired commander clapped him on the back, and the whiskey on the man’s breath sent James into a full-body sweat, heart hammering, vision narrowing. He excused himself and did not return. His wife, Cara, has asked him to stop at the grocery store on his way home; he cannot go anywhere near the beer aisle.

He has stopped seeing his friends from the ship. Several of them called, texted, invited him to a barbecue at the beach. He could not bring himself to answer. They were there; they know what happened. Being with them would mean acknowledging it out loud, and worse, it would mean standing near a cooler full of beer. The only place he feels somewhat safe is his house, but even there, a flickering bulb in the hallway sends him into a panic because it means he might be in the dark again. He has replaced every light fixture with bright LEDs and sleeps with the bedroom door cracked open.

James has started telling himself that he deserves to suffer for what happened. He cannot articulate exactly why. No one died, though several men were injured. Yet he has become certain that his own misery is a kind of payment—a way to balance the account from that night. He used to be a happy person, quick to laugh, the kind of officer junior sailors looked up to. Now he is miserable, and he has come to believe that is simply who he is. He no longer feels he belongs anywhere. On base, he is a stranger among men who did not live through that storm. At home, Cara tries to understand, but she cannot, and the distance between them has grown until he feels set apart from everyone he once loved.

What finally brought him into the clinic was a fitness report that included the words “withdrawn” and “difficult to count on.” His commanding officer told him he was being referred for evaluation. James is afraid—afraid that talking about it will make the images worse, afraid that admitting how much he avoids will get him medically separated from the only career he has known. But deeper than that, he is hoping for something he can barely name. A way to feel like he belongs to his own life again.
